6 EE PROJECTS WHERE
AI LIVES ON
YOUR BODY
Neural interfaces. Silent speech. Intent detection. Tactile augmentation.
All built on one platform. One PCB. Six applications.
1. Silent Speech Neural Interface — talk to AI without anyone hearing you, $60
2. EMG Prosthetic Hand — moves before your muscle contracts, $80
3. Gesture-Controlled AR Coding — type in mid-air, anywhere, $50
4. Emotion-Aware AI Companion — physiological context for AI, $30
5. Tactile Augmentation Glove — feel objects before you touch them, $45
6. Subvocal AI Commands — hands-free computing, silent input, $35
By @1nska • Electrical Engineer
@1nska  •  6 Physical AI Embodiment Projects  •  Page 2
THE PLATFORM
One core. Six applications. Endless possibilities.
Every project in this guide is built on the same core hardware platform. The Neural Bench architecture
combines an 8-channel 24-bit biosignal acquisition chip (ADS1299), a high-performance STM32H7
microcontroller, a Nordic nRF52 Bluetooth radio, and a LiPo charging system on a single PCB. What
changes between projects is the electrode placement, the firmware configuration, and the ML model
running on top. This is the philosophy: build the platform once, then build six (or sixty) applications.
Why this matters for your portfolio: Showing a recruiter six different applications
built on one platform demonstrates engineering judgment — you understand
abstraction, modularity, and platform thinking. That's worth more than six unrelated
demos.
@1nska  •  6 Physical AI Embodiment Projects  •  Page 3
THE STACK
Three layers. Master all three.
Every embodied AI project follows the same architecture. The analog layer captures biosignals from
the body. The DSP layer filters and conditions those signals. The AI layer classifies or regresses
against the conditioned signal to produce a decision. Understanding this stack — and being able to
design every layer — is what separates a hobbyist from an engineer who can ship a neural interface
product.
The analog layer is where most projects fail. Anyone can train an ML model. Few
can design a clean, low-noise, multi-channel biosignal acquisition front end. The
analog layer is your moat.

PROJECT 1
Silent Speech Neural Interface
Mouth words silently. AI reads your muscles. Text appears on screen.

Cost: ~$60
Difficulty: Advanced
Build Time: 2-4 weekends
Why This Matters
Meta acquired CTRL-labs for nearly $1 billion to build wrist-based gesture input. They have not built
silent speech yet. The reason is simple: their entire platform is locked into wrist EMG, and silent speech
requires reading muscle signals from the neck, jaw, and throat — a completely different body location,
different muscle group, and different ML model. The acquirer for silent speech is Apple, who needs a
private input method for Vision Pro and Siri, or defense contractors who need silent battlefield
communication. This is the flagship project. The one that gets you noticed.
The opportunity: Silent speech has the same demo impact as 'typing without a
keyboard' — but Meta isn't building it. A 3-4 year window exists before they pivot.
This is the project that defines a career or a startup.
System Architecture
@1nska  •  6 Physical AI Embodiment Projects  •  Page 5
How It Works
• 8 EMG electrodes around the neck and jaw: Specifically placed over the digastric, mylohyoid,
geniohyoid (chin), platysma (neck), and laryngeal muscles. Each muscle activates with different
phoneme groups — labial sounds (P, B, M) light up different muscles than dental sounds (T, D, N)
or velar sounds (K, G).
• ADS1299 simultaneous acquisition: Texas Instruments' gold-standard biosignal ADC. 24-bit
resolution, 8 channels sampled simultaneously at up to 16kSPS. Built-in PGA (programmable gain
amp) with selectable gain from 1x to 24x. Common-mode rejection ratio >100dB. This single chip
replaces what would otherwise be a discrete board with 8 instrumentation amplifiers.
• STM32H7 DSP: The MCU applies bandpass filtering (20-450Hz, the EMG band), notch filtering
(60Hz), and computes spectral features in real-time. Output: a continuous stream of 8-channel
feature vectors at 100Hz.
• Transformer model (EMG → text): A small encoder-decoder transformer (~2-5M parameters)
trained on paired EMG-to-text data. The encoder converts the EMG feature stream into a hidden
representation; the decoder generates the corresponding text. Runs on-device using TensorFlow
Lite Micro or CMSIS-NN.
• Bluetooth output: Decoded text streams to a paired device (phone, computer, AI assistant) via
BLE GATT. Latency from mouthed word to displayed text: under 500ms.
Key Design Decisions
→ Why neck/jaw electrodes instead of throat? Throat electrodes are awkward to wear and pick
up too much swallowing/breathing artifact. The neck/jaw region captures the same speech-related
muscles with a wearable form factor.
→ Why 8 channels minimum? Speech production involves dozens of muscles. 8 channels is the
practical minimum to distinguish phoneme classes — fewer channels lose information; more
channels add complexity without proportional accuracy gains.
→ Why a transformer instead of a CNN? Speech is sequential. The relationship between muscle
activations and meaning depends on temporal context — what came before. Transformers capture
long-range dependencies that CNNs cannot.

Build Steps
PCB design: Design a 4-layer flex PCB in KiCad. Layer stackup: signal-ground-power-signal.
Route the 8 differential EMG inputs as twisted pairs with matched length. Keep digital traces (SPI
between ADS1299 and STM32H7) away from analog inputs. Include a ground plane stitched with
vias. Manufacture at JLCPCB — about $4 for 5 boards.
Electrode array assembly: Sew or adhere 8 snap-on EMG electrodes onto a fabric neck collar.
Reference positions: 2 under the chin (mylohyoid/geniohyoid), 2 on the lateral neck
(sternocleidomastoid), 2 on the platysma, 2 near the laryngeal area. Plus 2 ground/reference
electrodes. Test impedance below 5kΩ at each site.
Firmware bring-up: Configure ADS1299 via SPI: gain x12, sample rate 1kSPS, all 8 channels
active. Implement a circular buffer that stores 1 second of data per channel. Apply digital filters:
20-450Hz bandpass + 60Hz notch. Verify with oscilloscope-equivalent display on connected laptop
— you should see clear EMG bursts when you mouth different phonemes.
Dataset collection: Build a training dataset by recording 1000+ short utterances. Software
prompts you to mouth a word silently; system records the EMG; you confirm the word. Save (EMG
sequence, label) pairs. For initial proof of concept, target a vocabulary of 100 common words. Use
this dataset to train your transformer.
@1nska  •  6 Physical AI Embodiment Projects  •  Page 7
Model training and deployment: Train an encoder-decoder transformer in PyTorch using your
dataset. Architecture: 4-layer encoder, 4-layer decoder, hidden dim 128. Quantize to int8 and
export to TensorFlow Lite Micro format. Deploy on STM32H7 with CMSIS-NN acceleration. Final
demo: wear the device, mouth a word from your vocabulary, watch text appear on a connected
phone.
Interview Questions:
→ Why is the ADS1299 specifically used for biosignal acquisition — what
differentiates it from a general-purpose ADC?
→ How do you handle electrode-skin impedance variation across users?
→ Why use a transformer model instead of CNN or RNN for EMG-to-text?
→ How would you handle out-of-vocabulary words?
→ What's the latency budget from mouthed word to displayed text?
→ How would you scale this to a continuous dictation use case?

PROJECT 2
EMG Prosthetic Hand with Intent Detection
5-finger control from forearm muscle signals. Faster than your own reflex.

Cost: ~$80
Difficulty: Advanced
Build Time: 2-4 weekends
Why This Matters
Commercial myoelectric prosthetic hands cost $20,000-$50,000 and offer 2-4 grip patterns. Modern
AI-driven prosthetics like the Ottobock bebionic or Open Bionics Hero Arm offer individual finger
control, but at higher prices and with significant calibration requirements. This project builds a 5-finger
prosthetic hand controlled by 8-channel forearm EMG with per-user CNN classification — the same
architecture used in research-grade prosthetics. Accessibility is the most meaningful application of
biomedical EE, and Medtronic, Abbott, and Össur all have active acquisition appetites in this space.
System Architecture
How It Works
• Forearm EMG array: Same 8-channel acquisition as the silent speech project, but with
electrodes placed in a ring around the upper forearm over the flexor digitorum superficialis and
extensor digitorum communis muscles. These muscles control finger flexion and extension; their
electrical signals appear at the skin surface as the user attempts to move individual fingers.
• Pre-amp + filter: Same DSP pipeline as silent speech — 20-450Hz bandpass with 60Hz notch.
Critical to remove motion artifact (slow drift below 20Hz) and electromagnetic interference (power
@1nska  •  6 Physical AI Embodiment Projects  •  Page 9
line noise at 60Hz).
• Per-user classifier (CNN): A small convolutional neural network trained on the user's specific
muscle activation patterns. Every person's forearm anatomy differs, so models must be
personalized. The training takes 60 seconds: the system shows the user a finger to flex; user
attempts the motion; system records the EMG pattern. Repeat for all 10 motions (5 fingers ×
flex/extend).
• Intent → finger mapping: Classifier output is a probability distribution over 10 possible motions.
The highest-probability motion is selected; intermediate-probability motions activate proportional
finger angles for smooth, continuous control.
• Servo drivers + 3D-printed hand: 5 servo motors (one per finger) driven by current-controlled
MOSFET drivers. Position feedback from each servo enables PID control. The hand is 3D-printed
using open-source designs (Inmoov, Open Bionics) with TPU tendons providing compliance.

Build Steps
Hand assembly: Print the open-source Inmoov or Hero Arm files in PLA. Print finger joints in TPU
for flexibility. Route TPU tendons from fingertips through the palm and out the wrist, terminating at
servo horns. Mount 5 servos on the forearm side of the wrist joint. Test mechanical motion: each
servo should produce one finger flex when actuated.
EMG sleeve fabrication: Sew 8 EMG electrodes into a compression sleeve at the forearm
positions described above. Wire each electrode to the snap connector on your Neural Bench PCB.
Adjust positioning until you get clean signals on all channels when the user attempts finger
movements.
Calibration session: Run the calibration software: the user wears the sleeve and attempts each
of 10 finger movements (5 fingers × flex/extend) for 5 seconds each. The software records EMG
signals and labels them. Total calibration time: ~60 seconds. The data is used to train the
user-specific CNN.
Model training: Train a small CNN (3 conv layers + 2 dense) on the calibration data. Input: 200ms
windows of 8-channel EMG (200 samples × 8 channels). Output: 10-class probability distribution.
Training runs on a laptop in <2 minutes; model is then deployed to the STM32H7 via USB.
Closed-loop control test: Wear the sleeve, attempt finger movements, watch the prosthetic hand
respond. Measure latency: time from EMG burst to servo motion start. Target: <100ms. If latency is
too high, optimize the inference loop (reduce model size, use quantization). Test individual finger
control vs. full hand grips. Document accuracy per finger.
Interview Questions:
→ Why do prosthetic hand classifiers need to be per-user instead of universal?
→ What's the difference between intent detection and motion detection in EMG?
→ How do you handle the case where the user wears the sleeve in a slightly different
position than calibration?
→ Why use current-controlled servo drivers instead of standard PWM control?
→ How would you add tactile feedback (sensation) for the prosthetic user?
→ What FDA regulatory pathway exists for medical-grade myoelectric prosthetics?

PROJECT 3
Gesture-Controlled AR Coding Interface
Sixteen-channel wrist EMG + screen-reading camera. Type anywhere.

Cost: ~$50
Difficulty: Advanced
Build Time: 2-4 weekends
Why This Matters
Meta's Neural Band shipped in 2025 with a vocabulary of approximately a dozen gestures. It works, but
it's a closed ecosystem locked to Ray-Ban Display glasses. The next frontier is full text input — typing
without a keyboard. Apple is researching this for Vision Pro. The competitive advantage: more
channels (16 vs. Meta's lower count), a camera that reads screen context to enable predictive
completion, and an open API that works across all devices. This is the project that demonstrates
competence with both biosignal acquisition AND multi-modal AI.
System Architecture
How It Works
• 16-channel EMG wrist band: Two stacked ADS1299 chips provide 16 simultaneous channels.
The wrist band is a ring of electrodes that wraps once around the forearm just below the elbow —
the location where individual finger control signals are strongest. Each finger creates a unique
16-channel pattern.
• Camera (back of hand or fixed): A small camera reads your screen content via OCR. This
provides context for predictive completion — if you're typing in a code editor and the system sees
@1nska  •  6 Physical AI Embodiment Projects  •  Page 12
Python syntax, it predicts completions in Python.
• Multi-modal sensor fusion: Two parallel streams (EMG features + screen context) feed into a
small transformer that fuses them. The EMG stream provides 'what you're trying to type'; the
camera stream provides 'what you should be typing in context.'
• Gesture + intent classifier: Maps EMG patterns to keystrokes. Tap index finger = 'I' key. Tap
middle finger = 'M' key. Pinch = 'space.' Swipe right = 'cursor right.' The mapping is learned
per-user through a 5-minute calibration where the user types known sentences while wearing the
band.
• USB-HID keyboard output: The device emulates a standard USB HID keyboard. To the host
computer, it looks like any keyboard — works with any OS, any application, no special drivers
required.

Build Steps
Dual ADS1299 setup: Cascade two ADS1299 chips via the DAISY_IN/DAISY_OUT pins. This
gives 16 simultaneous channels from a single SPI bus. Configure both chips identically: gain x12,
sample rate 1kSPS. Verify on a test signal that both chips sample synchronously.
Wrist band assembly: Embed 16 EMG electrodes in a TPU wrist band, spaced equally around a
60mm diameter (suitable for adult wrists). Each electrode connects to the snap header on the
PCB. The 17th and 18th positions are the ground and bias drive electrodes.
Camera integration: Mount the OV2640 camera module on the back of the hand or on a
desk-mounted stand pointing at the user's screen. Stream image data to STM32H7 via SPI at
10fps. Implement basic OCR (Tesseract Lite or a small CNN-based OCR) to extract text context
from the camera image.
Multi-modal model training: Collect training data: user types known sentences while wearing the
band. Record (EMG_features, screen_context, target_keystroke) tuples. Train a small transformer
that fuses both inputs and predicts the next keystroke. Quantize and deploy to STM32H7.
HID emulation: Configure the STM32H7 USB peripheral as a HID keyboard. When the classifier
outputs a keystroke prediction with high confidence, send it as a USB HID report. The host
computer receives it as if from a real keyboard. Test by opening Notepad/TextEdit and 'typing' with
the band on.
Interview Questions:
→ Why use two cascaded ADS1299 chips instead of a single chip with more
channels?
→ How does the camera context improve typing accuracy?
→ What's the latency from finger movement to keystroke output?
→ How would you handle the case where the user types faster than the inference
loop runs?
→ What's the difference between USB-HID and USB-CDC for this application?
→ How would you support keyboard layouts beyond QWERTY?

PROJECT 4
Emotion-Aware AI Companion Pendant
Multi-modal biosensor fusion. AI assistant adapts to your physiological state.
Cost: ~$30

Difficulty:
Intermediate-Advanced
Build Time: 2-4 weekends
Why This Matters
AI assistants today are emotionally blind. They respond the same way whether you're calm, stressed,
or exhausted. This pendant adds a physiological context channel — fusing heart rate variability, skin
conductance, jaw tension, and voice prosody — to produce a continuous emotional state estimate that
the AI can use. Imagine ChatGPT knowing you're stressed before you ask for help. Or your AI calendar
refusing to schedule a meeting when you're fatigued. This is the missing input modality for human-AI
interaction.
System Architecture
@1nska  •  6 Physical AI Embodiment Projects  •  Page 15
How It Works
• Multi-modal sensor array: The pendant houses 4 sensor channels — 2 ECG electrodes for
heart rate variability (HRV), 2 GSR electrodes for skin conductance, 1 EMG channel for jaw
muscle tension, and a small MEMS microphone for voice prosody analysis.
• Sensor fusion processor: An STM32 runs 4 parallel signal processing chains. HRV: R-peak
detection from ECG, time-domain and frequency-domain HRV metrics. GSR: AC-excited
conductance measurement with synchronous demod. EMG: standard biosignal pipeline. Voice:
pitch tracking, formant extraction, prosody features.
• Emotion classifier (CNN+LSTM): A hybrid network that ingests all 4 feature streams. CNN
extracts local features per stream; LSTM models temporal dynamics; final dense layer classifies
into emotional states (calm, focused, stressed, fatigued, excited).
• Bluetooth output: The classified emotional state streams via BLE to a connected phone or AI
service. APIs can subscribe to emotion state changes and adapt their responses accordingly. The
OpenAI API, for example, could receive emotion as a system message context: 'User is currently
stressed and fatigued.'

Build Steps
Sensor front ends: ECG: use the AD8232 dedicated ECG chip with 2 electrodes on the chest.
GSR: Wheatstone bridge with 100Hz AC excitation, synchronous demod for skin conductance (see
medical guide). EMG: standard pipeline for jaw muscle. Microphone: I2S MEMS mic feeds into
STM32 via direct DMA.
Feature extraction: ECG → R-peak detection → HRV metrics (RMSSD, pNN50, LF/HF ratio).
GSR → low-pass filter → tonic level + phasic responses. EMG → envelope detection → muscle
tension level. Audio → pitch + spectral features at 100Hz frame rate.
Emotion dataset collection: Build a training dataset: ask the user to record themselves in
different emotional contexts (relaxing music = calm, work stress = stressed, exercise = excited, late
evening = fatigued). Capture 5-10 minutes per state. Label and store. This is a per-user dataset —
emotions are personal.
Model training: Train CNN+LSTM in PyTorch using the user's labeled dataset. Architecture:
1D-CNN per stream (4 streams), then LSTM fusion, then dense classifier. Quantize and deploy.
Inference runs every 5 seconds.
BLE service + AI integration: Implement a BLE GATT service that exposes the current emotional
state. Build a phone app or system service that subscribes to this and passes emotion context to
AI APIs. Test: have the AI assistant respond differently when you wear the pendant in different
states.
Interview Questions:
→ Why fuse 4 sensor modalities instead of using just one?
→ What's the difference between tonic and phasic GSR responses?
→ How does HRV correlate with autonomic nervous system state?
→ What's the ethical consideration of streaming emotional state to AI services?
→ How would you handle user calibration without manual labeling?
→ What other applications exist for continuous emotion monitoring?

PROJECT 5
Tactile Sense Augmentation Glove
Feel objects from a distance. AI predicts touch before contact.

Cost: ~$45
Difficulty: Advanced
Build Time: 2-4 weekends
Why This Matters
Vision and touch are biologically synchronized — you see an object and your brain predicts what it will
feel like before you touch it. This glove makes that prediction explicit. A small camera identifies the
material and texture of the object you're reaching for; an AI model maps that material to a haptic
vibration pattern; the pattern plays on motors in the fingertips and palm. You 'feel' surfaces from 10cm
away. Applications: enhanced accessibility for the visually impaired, VR/AR interaction, training for
delicate manipulation tasks (surgery, archaeology, jewelry).
System Architecture
How It Works
• Camera on the back of the hand: A small camera (OV5640 or similar) points outward from the
back of the hand, capturing whatever the hand is reaching for. Streaming at 15fps to the on-glove
processor.
• IMU for hand pose: A 9-DOF IMU provides hand orientation and movement direction. This
contextualizes the camera image — knowing the hand is reaching forward changes what counts as
'about to be touched.'
@1nska  •  6 Physical AI Embodiment Projects  •  Page 18
• Material classifier: An edge ML model (MobileNet-Tiny or similar) trained to classify materials
from images: wood, metal, fabric, plastic, glass, paper, skin. Quantized and deployed on a
Raspberry Pi Zero 2W or similar edge compute platform mounted on the wrist.
• Distance + texture estimator: A second model estimates distance to the object (using parallax
from hand motion + IMU data) and surface texture (smooth, rough, grainy) from image features.
• Haptic pattern generator: Maps material+texture+distance to a vibration pattern. Wood = slow
steady pulse on the index fingertip. Metal = sharp, high-frequency pulse on the thumb. Smooth
surfaces = single steady vibration; rough surfaces = irregular pattern. Distance modulates intensity
— stronger as you approach.
• 16-channel PWM motor array: 16 ERM coin motors distributed on the fingertips (3 per finger)
and palm. Each motor driven by an independent PWM channel on a PCA9685 expander. The
pattern generator updates all 16 PWM values 100x per second.

Build Steps
Glove assembly: Sew 16 ERM motors into the glove substrate: 3 on each finger (proximal,
middle, distal phalanges), 1 on the palm. Route thin wires from each motor along the glove's
seams back to the PCB at the wrist. Use heat-shrink to insulate connections.
Computing module mount: Mount the Pi Zero 2W on the wrist with a 3D-printed bracket.
Connect the OV5640 camera via flat ribbon to the Pi's CSI port. Connect the BNO055 IMU via I2C.
Connect the PCA9685 via I2C to the same bus. Power everything from the LiPo through a buck
converter.
Material classification model: Train MobileNetV3-Small on a custom dataset of material images
(use Open Images dataset for initial training, fine-tune on your own samples). 7 classes: wood,
metal, fabric, plastic, glass, paper, skin. Quantize to int8 and deploy via TensorFlow Lite on the Pi.
Haptic pattern library: Define 7 distinct vibration patterns (one per material). Each pattern is a
1-second sequence of 16-channel PWM values. Patterns should feel distinct enough that the user
learns to associate them with materials within minutes of use. Test with blindfolded subjects.
Real-time loop: Main loop runs at 15fps: capture frame → classify material → estimate distance
→ look up haptic pattern → modulate by distance → write PWM values to PCA9685. Total latency:
<100ms from camera frame to haptic feedback.
Interview Questions:
→ Why use vibration motors instead of pneumatic or piezo actuators?
→ How do you handle multiple objects in the camera view?
→ What determines the spatial resolution of your haptic feedback?
→ How would you train the user to associate vibration patterns with materials?
→ What's the difference between this and actual texture sensing?
→ How does the IMU contribute to distance estimation?

PROJECT 6
Subvocal AI Command Interface
4 electrodes under the chin. 50 commands. Always-on. Hands-free.
Cost: ~$35

Difficulty:
Intermediate-Advanced
Build Time: 2-4 weekends
Why This Matters
Silent speech for full dictation is the moonshot. Subvocal commands for everyday computing is the
immediate product. A small 4-electrode patch under the chin runs always-on classification of 50
common commands: 'open email,' 'send message,' 'play music,' 'navigate home,' 'what time.' Mouth the
command silently — your phone or AI assistant responds within 100ms. This is the practical version
that ships in 6 months instead of 3 years. Apple, Google, and Amazon would all want this for their voice
assistants.
System Architecture
@1nska  •  6 Physical AI Embodiment Projects  •  Page 21
How It Works
• 4 EMG electrodes under the chin: Strategic placement over the digastric and mylohyoid
muscles — the muscles involved in jaw movement during speech. 4 channels are sufficient for a
fixed vocabulary of commands (unlike full speech which requires 8+).
• Ultra-low-power analog front end: Optimized for always-on operation. The MCU sleeps
between samples; an analog wake-up circuit (envelope detector + comparator) triggers full
processing only when subvocal activity exceeds threshold. Average power draw: <1mA, enabling
all-day battery life from a small coin cell.
• Keyword classifier: A small CNN trained on the fixed vocabulary of 50 commands. Output:
50-class probability distribution plus a 'silence' class. Inference runs only when wake-up triggers —
typically 100-500 times per day.
• Wake-word detection: The first word of any valid command serves as the wake-word. If 'Hey' or
'OK' or your custom trigger is detected, the system listens for the rest of the command. This
prevents false activations from random mouth movements.
• BLE command output: Detected commands transmit via BLE to your phone, smart watch, or AI
assistant. Standard intents like 'open_email' or 'play_music' map directly to OS-level actions.

Build Steps
Form factor design: Design a flexible PCB shaped like a small bandage (2cm x 4cm). 4 electrode
pads on the underside. Battery and electronics on the upper side. The whole assembly is meant to
be worn on the underside of the chin, held by adhesive or a thin neck strap. Manufacture with
JLCPCB's flex PCB service.
Wake-up circuit: Build an analog wake-up: envelope detector on one EMG channel feeds a
comparator with hysteresis. When signal exceeds threshold, comparator output wakes the MCU
from sleep. This eliminates the need to run the classifier continuously — saving 99% of the power
budget.
Command dataset: Define 50 commands covering common phone/AI assistant interactions.
Record 20+ examples per command from the user. Use data augmentation (time shifts, gain
variations) to expand the dataset 10x. Total training set: 10,000+ examples.
Classifier training: Train a small CNN: 3 conv layers + 1 dense + 1 softmax. Input: 1-second
4-channel windows. Output: 51 classes (50 commands + silence). Target accuracy: >95%.
Quantize to int8 for deployment. Model size: <100KB.
Integration with phone OS: Build an Android service or iOS app that listens for BLE commands
from the device. Each command maps to an OS-level intent: 'open_email' launches the email app,
'send_message' opens a compose window with the last contact, etc. Test the full pipeline: wear the
device, mouth a command silently, watch your phone respond.
Interview Questions:
→ Why use 4 channels instead of 8 for this application?
→ How does the analog wake-up circuit save power?
→ What's the false activation rate and how do you minimize it?
→ How would you add new commands without retraining the whole model?
→ What's the latency budget from mouthed command to phone action?
→ How would you handle multi-language support?
